## Abstract

Peanut oil cake biomass is a major by-product of oil industry and can be a suitable precursor for the production of biomass-based porous carbon. Herein, dual-stage activation, physical activation at 400°C, and chemical activation using KOH between 600 and 900°C are adopted to prepare hierarchical porous carbons (HPCs) from peanut oil cake biomass for use as electrode material in electrochemical supercapacitors. The textural and structural properties of the HPC were evaluated by N_{2}-adsorption/desorption, X-ray diffraction, Raman, FT-IR spectroscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. The prepared HPC inherited sufficient micropores and mesopores distribution with a maximum BET surface area of 640 m^{2}/g. The electrochemical properties of the HPC electrodes were evaluated by cyclic voltammetry, galvanostatic charge–discharge, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopic analysis. Among different HPC electrodes prepared, the carbon prepared at 800°C (HPC-P8) electrode material exhibited a high specific capacitance of 187 F/g at 0.5 A/g in 1M Na_{2}SO_{4} electrolyte in three-electrode systems. Symmetric supercapacitors were also fabricated using HPC-P8//HPC-P8 as positive and negative electrodes using 1M Na_{2}SO_{4} electrolyte, in a two-electrode cell configuration via split cell method. Maximum specific capacitance of 30 F/g was achieved with superior cycle stability of 93.8% capacitance retention over 5,000 cycles for the symmetric device. The device operated at a wide potential window (0–2.0 V) resulted in appreciable specific energy and power density of 15.89 Wh/kg and 493 W/kg, respectively. HPC-P8 had an ion diffusion coefficient of 7.79 × 10^{−8} cm^{2}/s which is higher than the other prepared carbon samples. The symmetric device showed relatively high charge storage capacity and cyclic stability without any material degradation. The fabricated prototype portable supercapacitor module was tested for red LED glow with maximum intensity brightness up to 4 min. Thus, the present study reveals that HPC derived from peanut oil cake biomass can behave as a promising electrode material for supercapacitor applications.

## 1. Introduction

In the present days, supercapacitors are gaining importance due to the need for the advancement of energy storage devices for societal applications. Supercapacitors constitute an effective energy storage behavior compared to the traditional capacitors and batteries. Supercapacitors, also known as ultracapacitors, are energy-storage devices that are used as stand-alone power source due to technological advancements and their needs. Supercapacitors have advantages over traditional condensers and batteries, for higher energy and power densities, faster charge and discharge rates, longer cycle life, and safer operation [1]. Because of these special qualities, supercapacitors are increasingly used in consumer electronics, industrial power management, and heavy electric vehicles. These features enable supercapacitors to be used as the primary or secondary power sources in various devices such as heavy machines and versatile gadgets [2]. Supercapacitors are divided into two types such as electric double layer capacitors (EDLCs) and pseudo capacitors based on the charge storage mechanism. These peanut oil cakes are known to possess a good source of protein and are used as one of the ingredients in animal feed.

Therefore, the present work is focussed on to preparepreparing HPC electrode material from peanut oil cake biomass by dual-stage activation method, and subsequently exploring the same for electrochemical performance by cyclic voltammetry, galvanostatic charge–discharge and electrochemical impedance spectroscopic analysis. The electrodes are also characterized to study their textural and structural properties by N_{2}-adsorption/desorption, X-ray diffraction, Raman, FT-IR spectroscopy, and scanning electron microscopy techniques. The electrochemical performances of PC electrode materials were analyzed in 1M Na_{2}SO_{4} aqueous electrolyte, as neutral electrolytes are ecologically well disposed in nature, eco-friendly, safe handling, low cost, and have good ionic conductivity. The electrochemical studies were performed by three-electrode technique as well as two-electrode technique for symmetric cell devices.

## 2. Experimental Section

### 2.1. Materials

Peanut oil cake was collected from the local oil mills, near Vellore Institute of Technology (VIT) at Kandigai, Chennai, and Tamil Nadu, India, for preparing HPC. Stainless-steel split cell purchased from MTI Korea Ltd., was used for symmetric cell studies. All the chemicals used in the experiment were of analytical grade. Polyvinylidene fluoride which was used as a binder was purchased from Sigma–Aldrich.

### 2.2. Synthesis of Peanut Oil Cake Derived Hierarchical Porous Carbon

Figure 1 shows the schematic representation of the HPC preparation. To prepare HPC materials, peanut oil cake biomass cake (PCB) was first washed with deionized water to remove dust and unwanted particles and subsequently dried in hot-air oven at 100°C. In the first stage, the dried PCB was subjected to precarbonization at 400°C for 4 hr at the heating rate of 5°C/min and cooled. Later, in the second stage, 30 g of this precarbonized carbon (HPC-PC) was added with 120 g of KOH (1 : 4 ratio) in required amount of water in continuous stirrer at 60°C for overnight and subsequently dried at 110°C for 2 hr in vacuum oven. The relationship between the current density and specific capacitance of the device is shown in Figure S2(b).

The cycle stability of the symmetric supercapacitor device was investigated up to 5,000 cycles, as shown in Figure 11(c) at a constant current of 10 A/g. The symmetric device displayed excellent cyclic stability with 93.8% retention of its capacitance values even after 5,000 cycles. The extraordinary stability of the symmetric device might be attributed to the electrode material’s microporous structure, which makes it easy for the migration of electrolytic ions and promotes greater adsorption/desorption processes. Figures S3(a) and S3(b) show the SEM images of HPC-P8 electrodes before and after 5,000 cycle stability. From the SEM images, it shows the surface of the electrode material remains the same without any modification and hence should be the structure of the electrode also even after 5,000 cycle stability.

## 5. Conclusion

This work proposed a concept of “Waste to Energy” applicable in the waste management. Using an effective and convenient method, hierarchical HPC from waste peanut oil cake has been produced and it exhibited an extraordinary electrochemical property with well-developed textural and structural characteristics. In comparison to all the prepared HPC samples, HPC-P8 exhibited excellent electrochemical performance in three-electrode system. The fabricated symmetric supercapacitor cell using HPC-P8//HPC-P8 electrode material showed 93.8% electrochemical stability over 5,000 charge/discharge cycles. The fabricated device operated in a wide potential window of 2 V in 1M Na_{2}SO_{4} showed high specific energy density of 15.89 Wh/kg at a specific power density of 493 W/kg. The glow of red LED from a prototype device proves that HPCs prepared from peanut oil cake will be a promising biomass material for high-performance electrode material in supercapacitor applications.

Abstract

Supercapacitors are widely recognized as energy storage solutions due to their high power densities and long cycle lives. Furthermore, there is growing scientific and technological interest in converting biomass waste into carbon materials for manufacturing supercapacitor electrodes. In addition to their abundance and cost-effectiveness, the appeal of carbons derived from biomass lies in their tunable porosity, which enables the rational design of carbon materials to achieve the desired performance of supercapacitors. Here, we present the synthesis of activated carbons from cashew nut shells via potassium hydroxide (KOH) activation at different temperatures (650, 750, and 850 °C). The resulting materials exhibited amorphous and predominant microporous structures. Increasing the activation temperature led to a rise in specific surface area from 1534 to 2034 m^{2}g^{−1}and an increased proportion of mesopores. The electrochemical properties of these activated carbons for supercapacitor applications were investigated by cyclic voltammetry, galvanostatic charge–discharge, and impedance spectroscopic techniques in a 1 M sodium sulfate (Na2SO4) electrolyte. Using a three-electrode system, the activated carbons treated at 750 °C exhibited a maximum specific capacitance of 106 F g^{−1}at a current density of 0.5 A g^{−1}with a good rate capability; they retained 75 % at 10 A g^{−1}over a 1.0 V voltage window. Furthermore, a symmetric supercapacitor coin-cell, fabricated with activated carbons treated at 750 °C as the positive and negative electrodes, demonstrated an energy density of 2.43 Wh kg^{−1}at a power density of 1002 W kg^{−1}. The cell exhibited 87 % capacitance retention at 1.0 A g^{−1}after 10,000 cycles. This work showcases the efficient and sustainable utilization of cashew nut shells as a carbon source for supercapacitor applications and highlights their value in a circular economy.
